# Phoenix Graceful Failover For Fast Rollback

Contributors: [Ritesh Garg](mailto:ritesh.garg@salesforce.com) [Kadir Ozdemir](mailto:kozdemir@salesforce.com)  
Updated: May 25, 2025

This document describes how Phoenix graceful (planned) failover can be used to execute fast rollback during deployment including release upgrade and configuration changes. It also identifies the work items to implement it.

## Overview

In Falcon, Phoenix team deploys two clusters (hbase1a and hbase1b). These clusters have bidirectional replication and have associated roles (ACTIVE and STANDBY). We plan to leverage these two clusters to ensure a fast failover to achieve under 30 min time to rollback for any issues during deployment. This document provides details on what is needed to accomplish this failover. 

## Current State

Although every core FD in Falcon has a pair of HBase clusters, they are not configured to failover the applications from one cluster to another. Also some of these cluster pairs are not completely synchronized meaning that the secondary clusters may have missing commits and these commits need to be replayed from the primary cluster. 2 FIs have clusters where replication is not enabled from 1a to 1b.

During graceful failover, the following actions will be executed:

1. Using Zookeeper, change the role of the primary cluster from ACTIVE to ACTIVE\_TO\_STANDY. This will signal Phoenix clients to stop accepting new connections and Phoenix servers to stop serving writes \[Dev Complete\]  
2. On the server side, wait for the replication queue on the primary cluster to drain \[Dev Complete\]  
3. Once the queue is drained, change the role from ACTIVE\_TO\_STANDBY to STANDBY and for current STANDBY to ACTIVE using zookeeper \[In Progress\]

## Approaches for Failover

There is a difference between regular deployment issues and bad changes requiring rollback. This is an important distinction. We may decide not to roll back for issues that can be fixed by an EBF and do not result in significant availability issues for the entire cluster. It is expected that really bad changes will be detected early by some decent FIT testing. Replication writes and Vagabond traffic will also help in detection. In the rest of this section, we assume that 1a is the current ACTIVE cluster and 1b is the current standby.   
For our normal release process, we have two alternative approaches.

### Failover only if needed

1. Deploy to 1a (ACTIVE) clusters using staggers and FIT tests. Bake after each stagger. If a bad change is observed, abort the deployment, fail over to 1b, and roll back 1a  
2. Deploy to 1b clusters using staggers and FIT tests if deployment is not aborted in step 1

### Always failover(Recommended)

1. Deploy to all 1b (STANDBY) clusters using staggers and FIT tests. If a bad change is observed, abort the deployment, and simply roll back 1b  
2. If the deployment is not aborted in step 1, fail over from 1a to 1b using staggers and bake after each stagger. If a bad change is observed, abort the deployment, fail back to 1a, and roll back 1b  
3. Deploy to all 1a clusters using staggers and FIT tests if the deployment is not aborted in step 2

### Comparison of approaches

There is no significant availability or performance impact difference between two approaches. It is expected that the “always failover” approach will take longer deployment time due one extra step for failover. However, the “failover only if needed” approach may not be able to make the rollback window (less than 30 min). Thus, the "always failover” approach is recommended.

| Parameters | Failover only if needed | Always failover (Recommended) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Availability | Availability issues during rolling upgrade of the active cluster due regions in transition. No availability issues due to failover if failover is not needed | Availability issues during failover but no availability issues due to rolling upgrade as rolling upgrade is not done on the active cluster |
| Deployment Duration | Less | More (due to the extra step for failover) |
| Rollback Time | Possibly not making rollback window as graceful failover from the active cluster with bad change may be too slow or unsuccessful | Expected to make rollback window as bad change would be likely be discovered before it is deployed to the active cluster |
| Performance Impact | General performance issues during rolling upgrade of the active cluster.  | Read performance degradation due to cold cache |

## Impact on Clients during Failover

* Vagabond will be able to write to and read from the standby cluster  
* Writes to the active cluster will be rejected  
* Reads from existing connections to the active cluster will make progress until the failover completes. If they are not completed before failover, they will fail as the connections on the active cluster will be closed

## Integration into Falcon Deployment Workflow

Currently in the Falcon release workflow, we have pre-decided staggers in Sedibus. These staggers currently execute deployment on 1b cluster for a given FD in 1 stagger and 1a in the next stagger. There are two factors which will change this:-

1. We plan to deploy to all Standby clusters first using staggers and FIT tests before targeting any Active clusters.  
2. In the next release, the standby clusters in the previous release will no longer be standby, they will be active. So hardcoding clusters in staggers might not work. 

To fix this, one possible solution is as follows:-

1. (Pre-Deployment Check) Add a stage before deployment to check if the current cluster state is Active or Standby. If it's Active, then no-op. If Standby, continue with the deployment.  
2. Update the staggers to include both 1a and 1b. For each stagger, based on the above pre-deployment check. Only 1 cluster will be affected.  
3. Add a new utility pipeline for executing failover.

Example walkthrough:-  
Lets assume at the beginning of release 1a clusters were in Active state and 1b were in Standby.

1. We use sedibus staggered release to go through all staggers, this will deploy to all 1b clusters.   
2. Now, we run the failover pipeline. After this 1b becomes Active and 1a becomes Standby.  
3. We execute the sedibus staggered release to go through all staggers, this will deploy to all 1a clusters now as 1a will be the Standby.

In the next cycle, 1a is Standby and 1b is Active, the same flow can be reused and user will perform the same execution to complete the release. Automatically, we will deploy to 1a(Standby) first and 1b next.
